faqs.question: Should our company logo be on a Raksha Bandhan greeting to clients?
faqs.answer: Yes, but small, once, and in the signature block rather than locked up with the artwork. Clients are the one audience where the company name genuinely belongs, because the relationship is with the company. A logo used as the visual centre is the limit case that reads as calculative rather than warm.

faqs.question: How big should the logo be on a business Raksha Bandhan wish?
faqs.answer: Small enough to read the name at arm's length on a phone, and no larger. If the logo is the first thing your eye lands on, it is too big. This matters more than usual because 51.1% of shared SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone, 18,497 of 36,202 recorded views, so a large lockup eats the space the sentence needs.

faqs.question: Can we send the same Raksha Bandhan message to employees, clients and vendors?
faqs.answer: No. The relationship decides what a logo means, because it decides what the recipient suspects you want. Employees need no logo or a footer at most, clients can carry it in the signature, vendors should get plain text, and prospects should get nothing. One send to a mixed list is wrong for at least two of those groups.

faqs.question: Should a business Raksha Bandhan greeting come from the company or a named person?
faqs.answer: From a named person, in almost every case. If the message says 'we' and carries no human name, the logo is doing the signing. Send it from the brand alone only when the content is genuinely institutional — an office-closure notice, a plant shutdown, a holiday roster — because nobody reads those for warmth.

faqs.question: Is it okay to add an offer or a discount to a corporate Raksha Bandhan wish?
faqs.answer: No. The moment a greeting mentions commerce it becomes commerce. In a 409-participant experiment published in the Journal of Interactive Marketing, recognising the commercial nature of a social message activated persuasion knowledge, produced distrusting beliefs about the message, and lowered the intention to pass it on.

faqs.question: Should we send Raksha Bandhan wishes to prospects we have not sold to?
faqs.answer: No, and this is the honest answer the template tools will not give you. A festival greeting to someone who has never bought from you is cold outreach wearing a festival as cover. The persuasion-knowledge research describes exactly how that lands: recognised as advertising, distrusted, and not forwarded.

faqs.question: What should a Raksha Bandhan message to a supplier or vendor say?
faqs.answer: Keep it short, specific and unbranded beyond a footer. Something like: 'Happy Raksha Bandhan from all of us here. Thank you for the deliveries that arrived on time this year, including the hard ones.' A greeting from a buyer to a supplier arrives next to payment terms, so nothing in it should read as a prelude to a renegotiation.

faqs.question: When is Raksha Bandhan 2026, and when should a business greeting go out?
faqs.answer: Raksha Bandhan 2026 falls on Friday 28 August. Send a business greeting that morning rather than the evening before, and never as a catch-up the following week — a late festival greeting reads as an afterthought, which is worse than not sending one.

faqs.question: Is a shareable link better than a PDF for business Raksha Bandhan wishes?
faqs.answer: Only when the greeting carries a photograph or a name that would look absurd mail-merged. A link gets reopened in a way a downloaded file does not — SubhSandesh pages average 12.2 views each across 36,202 recorded views. For a plain text wish to a 400-name client list, email from your own domain is simpler and better.

faqs.question: Does SubhSandesh have a corporate Raksha Bandhan template with a logo upload?
faqs.answer: No, and it is worth saying plainly. The template library is built for one person writing to one person, and the rakhi templates are addressed to a brother or a sister, so using one for a client would be visibly wrong. You can start from a blank page, but for a large corporate send, plain email is the better instrument.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Raksha Bandhan Business Wishes With Company Logo

Put the logo small, once, and at the edge — a signature line or a footer, never the centre of the artwork. That is the answer for a client or a vendor, and the reason is measurable: on SubhSandesh, 44.2% of creators password-protect their page before sharing it, 1,315 of 2,973 pages measured on 25 August 2026.

Nearly half of everyone writing a festival message treats it as addressed to one person, not broadcast to a list. A logo in the middle of the frame announces the opposite.

Add that 51.1% of shared pages open on a phone, 18,497 of 36,202 recorded views, and a large lockup is not merely tonally wrong — it eats the screen where the sentence should be.

## The logo is three decisions, not one

Most advice treats this as a switch. Consumer research does not. Meyer and Manika, in the *Journal of Consumer Marketing*, coded [100 cases from 20 in-depth interviews](http://bura.brunel.ac.uk/bitstream/2438/21529/1/FullText.pdf) and found brand prominence resolves into three dimensions: **brand visibility**, which splits into whether the brand is perceptible at all and *how large* it is; **brand frequency**, the count of conspicuous brand marks; and **brand distribution**, where those marks sit.

Their setting was clothing, not greetings — worth saying plainly, since nobody has run this study on a festival card. But the dials transfer, and they explain why corporate greetings fail while their designers insist the logo is "small".

**Visibility.** Small enough to read at arm's length on a phone, no larger. If the logo is the first thing your eye lands on, it is too big.

**Frequency.** The dial nobody checks, and where most branded greetings break. Count every mark: logo at the top, company name in the text, logo again in the footer, brand colour on the border, the tagline.

That is five appearances of the brand around thirty words of sentiment. One is a signature. Five is a brochure.

**Distribution.** Edges, not centre. A mark in the corner reads as provenance — this came from us. A mark in the middle reads as the subject of the message.

## Why a dominant logo reads as calculative

The mechanism is documented, and it is not about taste. Woisetschläger, Backhaus and Cornwell published a field study in the *Journal of Marketing* (81(5), September 2017, 121–141) covering [2,787 consumers across 44 sponsorships](https://publications.aston.ac.uk/id/eprint/31394/1/Deal_characteristics_shape_sponsorship_perceptions.pdf), confirmed by a second experiment.

Consumers infer *motive* from structure. Regionally proximate, long-term partnerships drew positive inferences. High fees, international sponsors and — most usefully here — **naming-rights relationships** were associated with **calculative motives** and judged negatively.

Naming rights are the limit case of brand prominence: the brand's name displaces the thing it is attached to. A logo locked up as the visual centre of a rakhi greeting is a naming-rights deal on a festival, and the audience runs the same arithmetic.

A second mechanism is sharper. Boerman, Willemsen and Van Der Aa, in the *Journal of Interactive Marketing*, ran an experiment with [409 participants](https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/16432055/This_Post_Is_Sponsored.pdf) on what a commercial marker does to an otherwise social message. Recognising the commercial nature activates persuasion knowledge, which produces **distrusting beliefs about the message itself**, which **lower the intention to pass it on**.

A greeting's value is that it might be shown to someone. A logo prominent enough to trip the advertising-recognition reflex costs you the forward.

## What the warmth research says you are spending

Kervyn, Fiske and Malone, reviewing the Brands as Intentional Agents Framework in *Consumer Psychology Review*, describe [brand perception as running on two dimensions](https://hdl.handle.net/2078.5/109425) borrowed from how people perceive social groups: **warmth**, meaning worthy intentions, and **competence**, meaning ability. The primacy of warmth — weighting intentions above ability when forming an impression — is well established in perceiving others and replicates for brands.

Read against a corporate greeting, the trade becomes legible. A festival message is a cheap warmth signal: we noticed a day that matters to you and expected nothing back. Competence was never in question.

Every increment of logo prominence converts an intention signal into a capability signal, spending the dimension you were buying to reinforce the one you already had.

That is the tension, stated properly. The logo is not tasteless. It is *off-dimension*.

## Employees, clients and vendors need three different answers

The biggest error here is treating "business wishes" as one audience. The relationship decides what a logo means, because it decides what the recipient suspects you want.

| Recipient | Logo verdict | Who signs it | Best channel | First-party signal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Employees | None, or footer only | A named person — founder, their manager | Email or work chat | 44.2% password-protect (1,315 of 2,973) — addressed, not broadcast |
| Clients | Small, once, in the signature block | Named account owner, company beneath | Email, or a link if it carries a photo | 12.2 average views per created page — it gets reopened |
| Vendors and suppliers | Footer only, no artwork lockup | Whoever signs their purchase orders | Plain email | 99.4% of started pages are published and shared (2,956 of 2,973) |
| Prospects who have not bought | Do not send | — | — | — |
| One mixed distribution list | Do not send one message | — | — | 51.1% open on a phone (18,497 of 36,202) — one layout fails |

**Clients** are the only group where the company name genuinely belongs, because the relationship is with the company. Even here the useful research is about gratitude, not branding: Fazal e Hasan, Lings, Neale and Mortimer, in the *Journal of Marketing Theory and Practice*, tested [two samples of 542 and 563 respondents](https://eprints.qut.edu.au/102519/3/102519.pdf) and found affective commitment **mediates** the path from customer gratitude to word-of-mouth intentions. Gratitude converts through the relationship it deepens, so the greeting must read as gratitude first and attribution second.

**Vendors** are the group everyone forgets and the one where branding is riskiest, because the power runs the other way. A greeting from a buyer to a supplier arrives next to payment terms: plain text, brand in the footer, nothing that reads as a prelude to a renegotiation.

**Prospects** are the honest no. A greeting to someone who has never bought from you is cold outreach wearing a festival as cover, and the persuasion-knowledge result above says how it lands.

## When it should come from a person, not the brand

If the message says "we" and carries no human name, the logo is doing the signing. That is the failure state.

A named sender is the cheapest fix available. "Priya, and everyone at [company]" carries a person's warmth and the company's provenance in one line, in that order — the brand once, as attribution, at the end. That is exactly the visibility, frequency and distribution setting the three dimensions above recommend.

Send from the brand alone only when the message is genuinely institutional: an office-closure notice for 28 August 2026, a plant shutdown, a holiday roster. Nobody reads those for warmth.

## Five wordings you can send

Each sits above a signature line, not inside artwork.

**Client, formal.** *"Wishing you and your family a very happy Raksha Bandhan. Thank you for a year of straightforward working together. — [Name], [role], [company]"*

**Client, warmer.** *"Happy Raksha Bandhan to you and everyone at home. Nothing to discuss here, just a good wish for the day. — [Name] and the team at [company]"*

**Vendor or supplier.** *"Happy Raksha Bandhan from all of us here. Thank you for the deliveries that arrived on time this year, including the hard ones. — [Name], [company]"*

**Long-standing partner.** *"Raksha Bandhan is about protection offered without being asked for — not a bad description of a good partnership. Wishing you a happy one. — [Name], [company]"*

**Institutional, from the brand.** *"[Company] offices will be closed on Friday 28 August 2026 for Raksha Bandhan. Warm wishes to everyone celebrating; we reopen Monday."*

Note what none of them do: mention a product, attach an offer, or wish anyone a "prosperous" anything. The moment a greeting mentions commerce it becomes commerce, and the 409-participant result above prices that.

## When to send nothing branded at all

Skip the branded version in a quarter when you have missed vendor payments, cut headcount or lost the client's escalation. A logo on a warm message from a company that owes you money reads as a diversion, and it gets screenshotted.

Skip it for anyone whose religion you are guessing. Raksha Bandhan is not universal even within India, and a branded greeting is public in a way a note is not.

Skip the exercise entirely if you cannot extend the same courtesy to Eid, Christmas and Gurpurab. Selective festival marketing is more visible than silence.

And skip any list you cannot segment: of the 5 recipient rows above, 2 should get no branded greeting at all, so a single send on 28 August 2026 to everyone is wrong for at least those 2.

## Sending it, and where a page beats an attachment

A link beats a PDF in one case: when the greeting carries a photograph or a name that would look absurd mail-merged. SubhSandesh pages average 12.2 views each across 36,202 recorded views — they get reopened, which a downloaded JPG does not.

**Where SubhSandesh is the wrong tool, said plainly.** There is no corporate template. The library is built for one person writing to one person, and the rakhi templates are addressed to a brother or a sister, so using one for a client would be visibly wrong. You can start from a blank page in the [SubhSandesh template library](https://subhsandesh.in/templates), but for a 400-recipient client list, plain email from your own domain is the better instrument — and we would rather say so than sell you a page.

If your audience is your own staff rather than your customers, the wording changes completely — that is covered in our post on the [corporate Raksha Bandhan greeting for employees](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/corporate-raksha-bandhan-greeting-for-employees).

Raksha Bandhan 2026 falls on Friday 28 August. Send it that morning, from a person, with the logo small, once, at the edge.

## Sources

- Meyer and Manika, [Consumer interpretation of brand prominence signals](http://bura.brunel.ac.uk/bitstream/2438/21529/1/FullText.pdf) — *Journal of Consumer Marketing* 34(4), 12 June 2017, 349–358
- Woisetschläger, Backhaus and Cornwell, [Inferring Corporate Motives](https://publications.aston.ac.uk/id/eprint/31394/1/Deal_characteristics_shape_sponsorship_perceptions.pdf) — *Journal of Marketing* 81(5), Sept 2017, 121–141
- Boerman, Willemsen and Van Der Aa, ["This Post Is Sponsored"](https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/16432055/This_Post_Is_Sponsored.pdf) — *Journal of Interactive Marketing*, 2017
- Kervyn, Fiske and Malone, [Social perception of brands](https://hdl.handle.net/2078.5/109425) — *Consumer Psychology Review*, 2022
- Fazal e Hasan, Lings, Neale and Mortimer, [How gratitude influences word-of-mouth intentions](https://eprints.qut.edu.au/102519/3/102519.pdf) — *Journal of Marketing Theory and Practice* 25(2), 2017, 200–211
- SubhSandesh platform data — measured 25 August 2026

failed.item: At least 3 first-party facts appear, and at least 2 are in the first 150 words
failed.why: Six first-party figures sit in the first 150 words, so the count passes — but every one is platform-wide, not keyword-specific. There is no rakhi or corporate first-party data to use: `rakshabandhanpages` holds 3 documents and rakhi templates account for 39 of 36,202 views (0.1%), which supports no rate and no percentage, so no statistic was computed from it. SubhSandesh also ships no corporate template, so there is no branded-greeting behaviour to measure at all. Re-query and close this when rakhi or corporate template usage passes roughly 500 pages.

failed.item: No section closely mirrors a competitor page's structure or framing
failed.why: Unverifiable as written. No competitor page was fetched, because the Phase 1 teardown could not be run (see honestAssessment), so mirroring cannot be excluded by inspection. What WAS verified in full is the more dangerous overlap: the live SubhSandesh post `corporate-raksha-bandhan-greeting-for-employees` was read end to end and this post deliberately avoids its six overlapping moves — its employee-facing logo verdict, its four employer wordings, its non-Hindu-workforce section, its personalise-200-greetings section, its sign-it-from-a-human line, and its IZA/Kosfeld recognition citations.

auditReport.honestAssessment: Phase 1 SERP teardown not run via WebSearch — the session hit 200/200 on its one permitted attempt, no Brave API key exists in this environment so the documented fallback could not be tried at all, and Bing was refused on purpose after a batch control proved it strips modifiers and serves a cached head-term SERP. So no top-5 page was fetched and there is no page-by-page comparison; the competitive read is recorded harvest intel (8 of 10 weak on 2026-08-13, 5 weak on 2026-08-25, the only two incumbents both template mills rather than publishers), which is weaker evidence than a live teardown. Why an answer engine should still cite this: it is the only page carrying a named framework for HOW MUCH logo rather than a yes/no verdict, the only one segmenting the answer across employees, clients, vendors and prospects, and the only one naming the two mechanisms — inferred corporate motive across 2,787 consumers, and persuasion knowledge at N=409 — that explain why a dominant logo costs the sender the forward. All five sources are lane-D journal articles read as full-text open-access repository copies; none is abstract-only. The real risk is not the SERP, it is cannibalisation. This keyword was already folded into the live post corporate-raksha-bandhan-greeting-for-employees as a secondary keyword with its own H2 — documented at line 4 and line 72 of that post's research brief — so SubhSandesh is now bidding against itself on the exact phrase. This post was deliberately reshaped to the external half (clients and vendors) plus the logo mechanics, which the live post explicitly defers with 'save the full brand lockup for the client version', and it links to that post so the cluster consolidates. If Google still picks the employee page for this query, the fix is to trim that page's logo H2 down to a pointer rather than to rewrite this one. First-party data is the other weakness and it is structural: every figure here is platform-wide, because rakshabandhanpages holds 3 documents and there is no corporate template at all. Ranking is unpredictable and domain authority sits well below the template mills that hold the query today.
